topics.title: Counting & Cardinality (1 to 20)
topics.summary: Understanding numbers 1–20, one-to-one correspondence, and comparing quantities.
sourceNotes: When counting objects, say the number names in standard order, pairing each object with one and only one number name.
The last number name said tells the number of objects counted (cardinality principle).
Each successive number name refers to a quantity that is one larger (n + 1).
topics.workedExample: Count 5 red apples on a tray: touch each apple one by one saying '1, 2, 3, 4, 5'. If we add 1 green apple, we now have 5 + 1 = 6 apples.
topics.commonMisconception: Skipping an object or double-counting the same object when items are arranged in a circle instead of a line.
learningObjectives: Understanding numbers 1–20, one-to-one correspondence, and comparing quantities.

topics.title: 2D & 3D Shapes in Our World
topics.summary: Identifying circles, squares, triangles, rectangles, spheres, and cubes by their attributes.
sourceNotes: Flat shapes are two-dimensional (2D): circles, triangles, squares, and rectangles.
Solid shapes are three-dimensional (3D): spheres (like a ball), cubes (like a dice), cylinders (like a can), and cones.
Shapes remain the same regardless of their size or orientation (a rotated triangle is still a triangle).
topics.workedExample: Look at a classroom clock and a sandwich cut diagonally: the clock is a circle (round, 0 corners) and the half-sandwich is a triangle (3 straight sides).
topics.commonMisconception: Thinking an upside-down triangle is no longer a triangle because the point is facing down.
learningObjectives: Identifying circles, squares, triangles, rectangles, spheres, and cubes by their attributes.

topics.title: Phonics, Letter Sounds & CVC Words
topics.summary: Connecting uppercase/lowercase letters to phoneme sounds and blending consonant-vowel-consonant words.
keyFormulas: Short Vowels: a, e, i, o, u
sourceNotes: Phonemic awareness is the ability to hear, identify, and manipulate individual sounds (phonemes) in spoken words.
Consonant-Vowel-Consonant (CVC) words like 'cat', 'dog', 'sun', and 'hat' are decoded by sounding out each letter and blending smoothly from left to right.
topics.workedExample: To read 'map': say /m/, then short /a/, then /p/. Blend slowly 'mmmaaaap' -> 'map'.
topics.commonMisconception: Confusing the letter name (e.g., 'see' for C) with its phonetic sound (/k/).
learningObjectives: Connecting uppercase/lowercase letters to phoneme sounds and blending consonant-vowel-consonant words.

topics.title: Living Things & The Five Senses
topics.summary: Distinguishing living from non-living things and exploring sight, hearing, touch, taste, and smell.
keyFormulas: Living things: Grow, Breathe, Need Food & Water
5 Senses: Eyes, Ears, Skin, Tongue, Nose
sourceNotes: Living things (plants and animals) grow, take in nutrients and water, respond to their environment, and reproduce.
Non-living things (rocks, toys, water) do not grow or need food.
Humans observe the world using five senses: sight (eyes), hearing (ears), smell (nose), taste (tongue), and touch (skin).
topics.workedExample: Compare a puppy and a plush toy dog: the puppy eats, breathes, and grows (living), while the plush toy stays the same and needs no food (non-living).
topics.commonMisconception: Believing clouds or cars are alive because they move.
learningObjectives: Distinguishing living from non-living things and exploring sight, hearing, touch, taste, and smell.

topics.title: Addition & Subtraction Within 20
topics.summary: Using number bonds, making ten strategy, and fact families to add and subtract within 20.
keyFormulas: Fact Family: a + b = c, b + a = c, c - a = b, c - b = a
sourceNotes: Addition combines two parts into a whole; subtraction finds a missing part when the whole and one part are known.
The 'Make Ten' strategy decomposes one addend to complete 10 with the other addend, simplifying mental calculation.
Addition and subtraction are inverse operations connected through fact families.
topics.workedExample: Solve 9 + 6: Take 1 from 6 to give to 9, making 10. Now add the remaining 5: 10 + 5 = 15.
topics.commonMisconception: Subtracting the smaller digit from the larger digit regardless of order (e.g., thinking 12 - 5 is the same as 15 - 2).
learningObjectives: Using number bonds, making ten strategy, and fact families to add and subtract within 20.

topics.title: Place Value: Tens and Ones
topics.summary: Understanding two-digit numbers as bundles of ten and leftover ones up to 100.
sourceNotes: In a two-digit number, the left digit represents the number of tens (groups of 10), and the right digit represents the ones.
Comparing two-digit numbers starts with the tens place: 52 > 39 because 5 tens is greater than 3 tens.
topics.workedExample: Decompose 64: the digit 6 is in the tens place (60) and 4 is in the ones place (4), so 64 = 60 + 4.
topics.commonMisconception: Thinking the '6' in 64 just means 6 instead of 60.
learningObjectives: Understanding two-digit numbers as bundles of ten and leftover ones up to 100.

topics.title: Plant Parts, Light & Sound Waves
topics.summary: How roots, stems, and leaves help plants survive, and how vibrations create sound and light enables sight.
keyFormulas: Plant System: Roots -> Stem -> Leaves -> Flower
sourceNotes: Roots anchor the plant and absorb water and minerals from soil; stems transport water upward; leaves capture sunlight to make food.
Sound is produced when objects vibrate (move rapidly back and forth), sending waves through the air to our ears.
Objects can only be seen when light illuminates them or when they give off their own light.
topics.workedExample: Pluck a stretched rubber band: you see it moving back and forth (vibrating) and hear a hum. Stop the vibration with your finger and the sound stops immediately.
topics.commonMisconception: Thinking our eyes send out rays to see in total darkness without a light source.
learningObjectives: How roots, stems, and leaves help plants survive, and how vibrations create sound and light enables sight.

topics.title: Complete Sentences, Nouns & Verbs
topics.summary: Building complete sentences with capital letters, end punctuation, naming words (nouns), and action words (verbs).
sourceNotes: Every complete sentence starts with a capital letter and ends with a punctuation mark (. ? !).
Nouns name a person, place, animal, or thing. Verbs describe an action or state of being.
topics.workedExample: 'The happy frog jumps into the pond.' -> Noun (subject): 'frog', Verb (action): 'jumps'.
topics.commonMisconception: Forgetting to capitalize the first word or using a period at the end of a question.
learningObjectives: Building complete sentences with capital letters, end punctuation, naming words (nouns), and action words (verbs).

topics.title: Place Value to 1,000 & Addition/Subtraction with Regrouping
topics.summary: Hundreds, tens, and ones; carrying and borrowing across place values.
sourceNotes: When adding two-digit numbers and the ones sum to 10 or more, regroup 10 ones into 1 ten and carry it to the tens column.
When subtracting and the top ones digit is smaller than the bottom ones digit, decompose 1 ten into 10 ones.
topics.workedExample: Calculate 47 + 36: Ones: 7 + 6 = 13 (write 3, carry 1 ten). Tens: 4 + 3 + 1 = 8 tens. Total = 83.
topics.commonMisconception: Forgetting to add the carried ten or forgetting to reduce the tens digit after borrowing.
learningObjectives: Hundreds, tens, and ones; carrying and borrowing across place values.

topics.title: Measuring Length, Telling Time & Counting Money
topics.summary: Using centimeters and meters, reading analog/digital clocks to 5 minutes, and counting coins.
keyFormulas: 1 hour = 60 minutes; each clock number = 5 minutes
sourceNotes: On an analog clock, the short hand points to the hour and the long hand points to the minutes (count by 5s around the dial).
Length must be measured by aligning the object's edge with the 0 mark on the ruler, not the physical edge of the plastic.
topics.workedExample: If the short hand is just past 4 and the long hand points to 6, count by fives to 6 (6 × 5 = 30): the time is 4:30.
topics.commonMisconception: Reading the minute hand by the face number directly (e.g., saying 4:06 instead of 4:30).
learningObjectives: Using centimeters and meters, reading analog/digital clocks to 5 minutes, and counting coins.

topics.title: States of Matter (Solid, Liquid, Gas) & Animal Habitats
topics.summary: Properties of solids, liquids, and gases, reversible heating/cooling changes, and biodiversity in habitats.
sourceNotes: Solids keep their own shape; liquids flow and take the shape of their container; gases spread out to fill all available space.
Heating ice melts it into liquid water (reversible change); baking batter into cake is an irreversible change.
Habitats (desert, rainforest, ocean, tundra) provide food, water, and shelter suited to specific adaptations.
topics.workedExample: An ice cube left in a warm bowl melts into liquid water. Putting that bowl back in the freezer turns it back into solid ice.
topics.commonMisconception: Thinking sand or flour is a liquid because it can be poured from a cup.
learningObjectives: Properties of solids, liquids, and gases, reversible heating/cooling changes, and biodiversity in habitats.

topics.title: Reading Comprehension, Main Idea & Compound Words
topics.summary: Identifying key details, central message, character motivations, and combining base words into compound words.
learningObjectives: Ask and answer who, what, where, when, why, and how to demonstrate understanding of key details in text
Identify the main topic of a multi-paragraph text as well as the focus of specific paragraphs
keyFormulas: Compound Word = Base Word 1 + Base Word 2 (e.g., sun + flower = sunflower)
sourceNotes: Good readers look for clues in both the illustrations and the text to infer character feelings and settings.
When encountering an unfamiliar compound word, break it down into the two individual words you already know.
Identify the main idea by asking: 'What is this paragraph mostly teaching me about?'
topics.workedExample: Read: 'Leo packed his umbrella and stepped outside. Dark clouds covered the blue sky.' Question: What will the weather be like? Clues: Dark clouds + umbrella -> Inference: It is about to rain.
topics.commonMisconception: Confusing a supporting detail with the overall main idea of the story.

topics.title: Multiplication & Division Foundations
topics.summary: Equal groups, arrays, area models, and inverse relationship between multiplication and division.
keyFormulas: a × b = a groups of b
sourceNotes: Multiplication represents repeated addition of equal groups: 4 × 6 means 6 + 6 + 6 + 6 = 24.
The Commutative Property states that changing factor order does not change the product (4 × 6 = 6 × 4).
The Distributive Property breaks apart tough facts: 7 × 8 = 7 × (5 + 3) = 35 + 21 = 56.
topics.workedExample: A garden has 4 rows of 8 tomato plants. Total plants = 4 × 8 = 32 plants. If shared equally into 4 baskets, each basket gets 32 ÷ 4 = 8.
topics.commonMisconception: Confusing perimeter (distance around: 2L + 2W) with area (space inside: L × W).
learningObjectives: Equal groups, arrays, area models, and inverse relationship between multiplication and division.

topics.title: Understanding Fractions on a Number Line
topics.summary: Partitioning wholes into equal parts, numerator vs. denominator, and equivalent fractions.
keyFormulas: Fraction = Numerator (parts selected) / Denominator (total equal parts)
sourceNotes: A fraction represents equal parts of a whole or a precise location on a number line between 0 and 1.
When comparing fractions with the same numerator, the fraction with the smaller denominator is larger (1/3 > 1/6 because each third is a bigger piece).
topics.workedExample: Divide a number line from 0 to 1 into 4 equal jumps. Each jump is 1/4. Two jumps land at 2/4, which is the exact midpoint 1/2.
topics.commonMisconception: Thinking 1/8 is bigger than 1/4 because 8 is bigger than 4.
learningObjectives: Partitioning wholes into equal parts, numerator vs. denominator, and equivalent fractions.

topics.title: Forces, Magnetism & Weather Patterns
topics.summary: Balanced and unbalanced forces, friction, magnetic poles, and the water cycle.
sourceNotes: A force is a push or a pull that can start motion, stop motion, or change an object's direction.
Magnets exert non-contact force on ferromagnetic metals (iron, nickel, cobalt). North and South poles attract; identical poles repel.
Friction opposes motion between two surfaces sliding past each other.
topics.workedExample: Two students pull a rope with 50 N left and 50 N right: forces are balanced, so the rope stays still. If the right side pulls with 70 N, the rope accelerates right.
topics.commonMisconception: Thinking all shiny metals (like aluminum foil or copper coins) stick to magnets.
learningObjectives: Balanced and unbalanced forces, friction, magnetic poles, and the water cycle.

topics.title: Text Structure, Cause & Effect and Prefixes/Suffixes
topics.summary: Analyzing cause-and-effect relationships in informational texts and decoding vocabulary with prefixes (un-, re-, pre-) and suffixes (-ful, -less).
learningObjectives: Describe the logical connection between particular sentences and paragraphs in a text (e.g., comparison, cause/effect)
Determine the meaning of the new word formed when a known affix is added to a known word
keyFormulas: Prefix 'un-' = not (unhappy = not happy); 're-' = again (rewrite = write again)
sourceNotes: Signal words like 'because', 'therefore', 'as a result', and 'since' indicate cause and effect relationships.
Affixes modify root words: removing the prefix or suffix reveals the base word's root meaning.
Text features like headings, captions, and glossaries guide navigation through non-fiction text.
topics.workedExample: Sentence: 'Because the temperatures dropped below freezing overnight, the puddle turned into a sheet of ice.' Cause: Temperatures dropped below freezing. Effect: Puddle turned into ice.
topics.commonMisconception: Reversing cause and effect: thinking the effect caused the original event.

topics.title: Multi-Digit Multiplication, Long Division & Decimals
topics.summary: Area model multiplication, division with remainders, fraction equivalence, and tenths/hundredths.
sourceNotes: Multi-digit multiplication uses partial products based on place value before summing the results.
Decimals extend the base-10 place value system to the right of the decimal point: tenths (1/10) and hundredths (1/100).
topics.workedExample: Convert 3/4 to a decimal: multiply numerator and denominator by 25 to get 75/100, which is written as 0.75.
topics.commonMisconception: Thinking 0.35 is greater than 0.4 because 35 > 4 (ignoring that 0.4 = 0.40).
learningObjectives: Area model multiplication, division with remainders, fraction equivalence, and tenths/hundredths.

topics.title: Lines, Angles & Symmetry
topics.summary: Measuring acute, right, obtuse, and straight angles with a protractor; parallel and perpendicular lines.
sourceNotes: Parallel lines never intersect and stay the same distance apart; perpendicular lines intersect at a 90° right angle.
Two angles that form a straight line add up to 180° (supplementary); two angles forming a right corner add up to 90° (complementary).
topics.workedExample: If a right angle (90°) is split into two angles and one measures 35°, the other angle is 90° - 35° = 55°.
topics.commonMisconception: Reading the wrong scale (inner vs. outer) on a protractor, claiming an acute angle is 140° instead of 40°.
learningObjectives: Measuring acute, right, obtuse, and straight angles with a protractor; parallel and perpendicular lines.

topics.title: Energy Transfer, Simple Circuits & Earth's Rock Cycle
topics.summary: Forms of energy (kinetic, thermal, electrical), closed loops in circuits, and weathering/erosion.
sourceNotes: Energy cannot be created or destroyed; it transforms from one form to another (e.g., chemical energy in a battery -> electrical energy -> light and heat in a bulb).
Weathering breaks down rocks in place through wind, water, or ice; erosion transports those sediment particles to new locations.
topics.workedExample: When water freezes inside a rock crack, it expands and splits the rock (ice wedging / physical weathering), and river flow carries the pebbles downstream (erosion).
topics.commonMisconception: Confusing weathering (breaking down rock) with erosion (moving the broken rock).
learningObjectives: Forms of energy (kinetic, thermal, electrical), closed loops in circuits, and weathering/erosion.

topics.title: Textual Evidence, Theme Identification & Prepositions
topics.summary: Citing evidence to support inferences, identifying the author's theme or moral, and mastering prepositional phrases.
learningObjectives: Refer to details and examples in a text when explaining what the text says explicitly and when drawing inferences
Determine a theme of a story, drama, or poem from details in the text
keyFormulas: Theme = Universal message about life (not just a one-word topic)
Claim + Textual Evidence ('In paragraph 3, the author states...') = Grounded Answer
sourceNotes: A theme must apply beyond the specific characters to real human experiences (e.g., 'True friendship requires honesty', not just 'frogs').
Direct quotations must be bounded by quotation marks and accurately mirror the source text.
Prepositional phrases add detail answering where, when, or how (e.g., 'under the bridge', 'after sunset').
topics.workedExample: Prompt: What is the theme of 'The Boy Who Cried Wolf'? Answer: Honesty is essential because if you frequently lie, people will not believe you even when you tell the truth.
topics.commonMisconception: Confusing the plot summary ('A wolf ate the sheep') with the moral/theme of the passage.

topics.title: Operations with Fractions & Mixed Numbers
topics.summary: Adding, subtracting, multiplying, and dividing fractions with unlike denominators.
sourceNotes: To add or subtract fractions with unlike denominators, first find the Least Common Multiple (LCM) of the denominators to create equivalent fractions.
Multiplying fractions multiplies numerators together and denominators together — no common denominator is needed.
topics.workedExample: Add 2/3 + 1/4: LCM of 3 and 4 is 12. Convert to 8/12 + 3/12 = 11/12.
topics.commonMisconception: Adding both numerators and denominators directly (writing 2/3 + 1/4 = 3/7).
learningObjectives: Adding, subtracting, multiplying, and dividing fractions with unlike denominators.

topics.title: 3D Volume, Order of Operations (PEMDAS) & Coordinate Plane
topics.summary: Calculating volume of rectangular prisms, evaluating parentheses/exponents, and plotting (x, y) pairs.
keyFormulas: Volume = Length × Width × Height (V = l × w × h)
sourceNotes: Volume measures the 3D space inside a solid in cubic units (cm³, m³). For a rectangular prism, V = Base Area × Height.
On the coordinate plane, an ordered pair (x, y) locates a point by moving horizontally along the x-axis first, then vertically along the y-axis.
topics.workedExample: Evaluate 20 - 3 × (2 + 4): First parentheses (2 + 4 = 6), then multiplication (3 × 6 = 18), finally subtraction (20 - 18 = 2).
topics.commonMisconception: Performing subtraction before multiplication in 20 - 3 × 6 (getting 17 × 6 = 102 instead of 2).
learningObjectives: Calculating volume of rectangular prisms, evaluating parentheses/exponents, and plotting (x, y) pairs.

topics.title: Conservation of Matter, Food Webs & Solar System
topics.summary: Producers, consumers, decomposers, conservation of mass in mixtures, and Earth's rotation vs. orbit.
keyFormulas: Photosynthesis: Sunlight + CO₂ + H₂O -> Glucose + O₂
sourceNotes: In any physical or chemical change, the total weight (mass) of matter is conserved — dissolving 10 g of salt in 100 g of water yields 110 g of salt water.
Energy in an ecosystem flows from the Sun to producers (plants), then to herbivores, carnivores, and decomposers.
Earth's 24-hour rotation on its axis causes day and night and the apparent movement of shadows.
topics.workedExample: When 5 g of sugar dissolves completely in 200 g of tea, the sugar particles spread out invisibly, but the scale reads exactly 205 g.
topics.commonMisconception: Thinking dissolved sugar disappears and loses its mass because it is no longer visible.
learningObjectives: Producers, consumers, decomposers, conservation of mass in mixtures, and Earth's rotation vs. orbit.

topics.title: Algorithms, Loops & Conditional Logic
topics.summary: Step-by-step instructions, repeat loops, if/else decisions, and debugging sequences.
sourceNotes: An algorithm is an unambiguous, ordered list of steps designed to solve a problem or complete a task.
Loops repeat a block of instructions multiple times to avoid redundant code; conditionals (if/else) make decisions based on boolean conditions.
topics.workedExample: To draw a square with a robot turtle: Repeat 4 times: [Move Forward 100 steps, Turn Right 90 degrees].
topics.commonMisconception: Assuming a computer can infer missing steps that weren't explicitly written in the algorithm.
learningObjectives: Step-by-step instructions, repeat loops, if/else decisions, and debugging sequences.

topics.title: Point of View, Figurative Language & Argumentative Essays
topics.summary: Analyzing first vs. third person perspectives, metaphors, similes, and constructing 5-paragraph thesis-driven essays.
learningObjectives: Write opinion pieces on topics or texts, supporting a point of view with reasons and information
Explain how an author's point of view or purpose shapes the content and style of a text
keyFormulas: Simile: Comparison using 'like' or 'as' (e.g., brave as a lion)
Metaphor: Direct comparison stating one thing IS another (e.g., time is a thief)
Essay Structure = Hook + Thesis -> 3 Evidence Paragraphs -> Restated Conclusion
sourceNotes: First-person narrator uses 'I/we' and offers subjective emotional access; third-person omniscient knows all characters' thoughts.
Every body paragraph in an argument essay must begin with a clear topic sentence directly linked to the thesis statement.
Transition words (furthermore, however, in contrast, consequently) build logical progression.
topics.workedExample: Thesis: 'School recess should be extended because it enhances physical health, boosts concentration, and builds social skills.' Body paragraph 1 expands physical health with research statistics.
topics.commonMisconception: Asserting an opinion without providing supporting evidence or citations from the text.
